```{r setup, include=FALSE}

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(readr)
library(janitor)
library(here)
library(haven)
library(modelsummary)
library(ggeffects)
library(margins)
```

```{r Step 0: data ingestion, include=TRUE}
cmps_merged <- read_csv(here("cmps_merged_civicorgdata_2024.csv"))

#Create Control Variables
# Create other factor variables
cmps_merged$gender_factor <- factor(cmps_merged$s14, 
                                   levels = 1:3,
                                   labels = c("Man", "Woman", "Non-binary"))

cmps_merged$race_factor <- factor(cmps_merged$qraceid,
                                 levels = 1:6,
                                 labels = c("White",
                                           "Latino", 
                                           "Black",
                                           "Asian",
                                           "Native American",
                                           "MENA"))

cmps_merged$income_factor <- factor(cmps_merged$hhinc, 
                                   levels = 1:5,
                                   labels = c("Less than $39k", "$40k-$59k", 
                                             "$60k-$99k", "$100k+", "Don't know"))

cmps_merged$income_ordinal <- ifelse(cmps_merged$s20 == 13, NA, cmps_merged$s20)

cmps_merged$agenum <- 2024 - cmps_merged$s2

cmps_merged$age_c <- cmps_merged$agenum - mean(
  cmps_merged$agenum,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

cmps_merged$education_factor <- factor(cmps_merged$s17, 
                                      levels = 1:7,
                                      labels = c("Grades 1-8", "Some high school", 
                                                "High school graduate or GED", "Some college",
                                                "Associates, 2-year degree", "Bachelors, 4-year degree",
                                                "Post-graduate degree"))

cmps_merged$age_factor <- factor(cmps_merged$agecat, 
                                levels = 1:5,
                                labels = c("16-17 yrs", "18-29 yrs", "30-44 yrs", 
                                          "45-64 yrs", "65+ yrs"))

cmps_merged$region_factor <- factor(cmps_merged$region, 
                                   levels = 1:4,
                                   labels = c("Midwest", "Northeast", "South", "West"))

cmps_merged$urban_factor <- factor(cmps_merged$s24, 
                                  levels = 1:5,
                                  labels = c("Large urban area", "Large suburb near large city",
                                            "Small suburb near small town or city", 
                                            "Small town or small city", "Rural area"))

cmps_merged$q25b <- max(cmps_merged$q25b, na.rm = TRUE) + min(cmps_merged$q25b, na.rm = TRUE) - cmps_merged$q25b

# Create binary outcome: 1 = responded "1" (optimistic), 0 = otherwise
cmps_merged$q30_optim <- ifelse(cmps_merged$q30 == 1, 1,
                          ifelse(is.na(cmps_merged$q30), NA, 0))

# Create binary outcome: 1 = responded "2", 0 = otherwise
cmps_merged$q30_pess <- ifelse(cmps_merged$q30 == 2, 1,
                         ifelse(is.na(cmps_merged$q30), NA, 0))
```

```{r Step 1: Initial Model on Civic Opportunity Levels and Voter Turnout, include=TRUE}
#I coded this to include those who voted as those who were certain and those who thought they were voted but were uncertain
cmps_merged$voted_2024 <- as.numeric(cmps_merged$q12 == 3 | cmps_merged$q12 == 4)


#Naive Model on Voter Turnout
model_vote_2024 <- lm(voted_2024 ~ opc, data = cmps_merged)
summary(model_vote_2024)

#Logistic Regression Version
turnout_logit_1 <- glm(
  voted_2024 ~ opc,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = cmps_merged
)

summary(turnout_logit_1)

#Controlled Model - Robustness Check
model_vote_2024_controlled <- lm(voted_2024 ~ opc + race_factor + gender_factor + income_ordinal + 
                               education_factor + age_c + region_factor + urban_factor + pid7, 
                               data = cmps_merged)
summary(model_vote_2024_controlled)

## Logistic Version
turnout_logit_full <- glm(
  voted_2024 ~ opc * age_c + race_factor + gender_factor +
    income_ordinal + education_factor + region_factor +
    urban_factor + pid7,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = cmps_merged
)

summary(turnout_logit_full)

#Model That includes Less Covariates Due to Model Overfit
model_minimal <- lm(voted_2024 ~ opc + age_c + race_factor + gender_factor + 
                   income_factor + pid7, data = cmps_merged)
summary(model_minimal)


## Logistic Version
turnout_logit_2 <- glm(
  voted_2024 ~ opc + age_c + race_factor + gender_factor +
    income_factor + pid7,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = cmps_merged
)

summary(turnout_logit_2)

#Model that Interacts Civic Opportunity with Age
model_2024_interaction <- lm(voted_2024 ~ opc * age_c + race_factor + gender_factor + 
                            income_ordinal + education_factor + region_factor + 
                            urban_factor + pid7, data = cmps_merged)
summary(model_2024_interaction)


#Minimal Model that Interacts Civic Opportunity with Age
model_2024_interaction_minimal <- lm(voted_2024 ~ opc * age_c + race_factor + gender_factor +
    income_factor + pid7, data = cmps_merged)
summary(model_2024_interaction_minimal)

## Logistic Version
turnout_logit_3 <- glm(
  voted_2024 ~ opc * age_c + race_factor + gender_factor +
    income_factor + pid7,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = cmps_merged
)

summary(turnout_logit_3)

#Across baseline models, county-level civic opportunity structure is positively associated with self-reported turnout in the 2024 election. This relationship appears in both linear probability and logistic specifications and remains statistically significant after adjusting for demographic, socioeconomic, partisan, and geographic controls. Models that interact opportunity structure with age indicate that the turnout association is stronger among younger respondents: the interaction is negative and statistically significant in the fully specified linear model and negative but only marginally significant in the logistic models. Taken together, these results suggest that denser civic organizational environments are associated with higher turnout overall, with particularly strong benefits for younger adults (CHATGPT)

```

```{r Step 1.5: Restricting the Sample to just Those Who Are Fully Sure About Voting in 2024, include=TRUE}
#As a robustness check, we re-estimated the turnout models using a stricter outcome that coded only respondents who reported being certain they voted in 2024 as voters. Across these models, civic opportunity structure remained positively associated with turnout, indicating that the main relationship is not driven by respondents with uncertain self-reports. At the same time, the interaction between opportunity structure and age became smaller and statistically insignificant across specifications. This suggests that while the positive association between local civic opportunity structure and turnout is robust, evidence that this relationship is especially strong among younger respondents is more sensitive to how turnout is operationalized (CHATGPT)
```
```{r Step 2: Comparing Stratifying the Sample vs Doing an Interaction Model on the Intersection of Civic Opportunity, Age, and Political Interest, include=TRUE}
# Young people model
# Option A: Focus on young people (say, under 40) and test civic density effect on optimism
young_sample <- subset(cmps_merged, agenum < 40)

model_young_political_interest <- lm(q25b ~ opc + race_factor + gender_factor + 
                                    income_factor + education_factor + region_factor + 
                                    urban_factor + pid7, data = young_sample)


# Full interaction model
model_political_interest_interaction <- lm(q25b ~ opc * age_c + race_factor + gender_factor + 
                                          income_factor + education_factor + region_factor + 
                                          urban_factor + pid7, data = cmps_merged)

summary(model_young_political_interest)
summary(model_political_interest_interaction)

# Full interaction model
model_political_interest_interaction_age_centered <- lm(q25b ~ opc * age_c + race_factor + gender_factor + 
                                          income_factor + education_factor + region_factor + 
                                          urban_factor + pid7, data = cmps_merged)
summary(model_political_interest_interaction_age_centered)

#Minimal Model Check
# Young people model
minimal_young_political_interest <- lm(q25b ~ opc + race_factor + gender_factor + 
                                    income_ordinal + pid7, data = young_sample)

# Full interaction model
minimal_political_interest_interaction <- lm(q25b ~ opc * agenum + race_factor + gender_factor + 
                                          income_ordinal + pid7, data = cmps_merged)

summary(minimal_young_political_interest)
summary(minimal_political_interest_interaction)

model_political_interest_interaction_minimal_age_centered <- lm(q25b ~ opc * age_c + race_factor + gender_factor + 
                                          income_factor + education_factor + region_factor + 
                                          urban_factor + pid7, data = cmps_merged)
summary(model_political_interest_interaction_minimal_age_centered)
#The civic opportunity environment appears to matter for younger adults, but its effect may operate less through immediate turnout and more through antecedents of participation such as political interest or attentiveness to public affairs. To probe why the relationship between civic opportunity structure and turnout among younger respondents is weaker in logistic models, I examined whether county-level opportunity structure predicts political attentiveness. Among respondents under age 40, higher opportunity structure is significantly associated with more frequent news-following, controlling for demographic, socioeconomic, geographic, and partisan factors (b = -0.129, p < .01). Because lower values of the dependent variable indicate more frequent attention to news, this result suggests that denser civic environments may foster political interest among younger adults even when their effect on turnout is not fully direct. This pattern is consistent with the idea that civic opportunity structure affects youth participation indirectly: it may cultivate attentiveness and engagement before translating into electoral participation. Among people under 40, higher levels of civic opportunity in the local environment are significantly associated with greater political/news attentiveness. This helps explain why the effect of opportunity structure on turnout may be muted or only marginally significant in younger samples: civic environments may be shaping political interest first, with turnout as a later or less direct outcome. o assess whether the relationship between civic opportunity structure and political attentiveness varies by age, I estimated a model of news-following frequency including an interaction between county-level opportunity structure and age. Because lower values of the dependent variable indicate more frequent news-following, the negative coefficient on opportunity structure indicates greater political attentiveness. The interaction between opportunity structure and age is positive and statistically significant (b = 0.0037, p = .032), indicating that the negative association between opportunity structure and news-following weakens as respondents get older. In substantive terms, higher civic opportunity structure is associated with more frequent news-following most strongly among younger respondents, with the relationship attenuating across the life course.

#The average-age effect of opportunity structure is modest and only marginally significant, but this masks substantial age heterogeneity. The significant interaction indicates that the association is considerably stronger among younger respondents and attenuates as age increases. If civic opportunity structure is more strongly related to political attentiveness among younger adults than among older adults, then its effect on turnout among the young may be operating indirectly through engagement and interest rather than showing up as a large direct turnout effect. In a fully specified model of political attentiveness, measured by frequency of following the news, the interaction between county-level civic opportunity structure and age is positive and statistically significant (b = 0.0040, p = .019). Because lower values of the dependent variable indicate more frequent news-following, this result implies that the negative association between opportunity structure and attentiveness weakens as age increases. In the age-centered specification, the main effect of opportunity structure at the sample mean age is negative but only marginally significant (b = -0.054, p = .065), indicating that average effects obscure meaningful age heterogeneity. Taken together, the findings suggest that denser civic environments are more strongly associated with political attentiveness among younger adults than among older respondents.

```

```{r Step 3: Look at the importance of Valence on the Economy to Age's Interaction with Civic Opportunity, include=TRUE}


# Logistic regression with age interaction
model_optimism <- glm(q30_optim ~ opc * age_c + race_factor + gender_factor +
                        income_factor + education_factor + region_factor +
                        urban_factor + pid7,
                      data = cmps_merged,
                      family = binomial(link = "logit"))

summary(model_optimism)


# Logistic regression with interaction
model_pess <- glm(q30_pess ~ opc * age_c + race_factor + gender_factor +
                    income_factor + education_factor + region_factor +
                    urban_factor + pid7,
                  data = cmps_merged,
                  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

summary(model_pess)

#Checking in with minimal model
model_young_optimism_minimal <- lm(q30 ~ opc + race_factor + gender_factor + 
                   income_ordinal + pid7, data = young_sample)

model_optimism_interaction_minimal <- lm(q30 ~ opc * age_c + race_factor + gender_factor + 
                                income_ordinal + pid7, data = cmps_merged)

summary(model_young_optimism_minimal)
summary(model_optimism_interaction_minimal)

#Interacting Between Pessimism and Political Attentiveness
cor(cmps_merged$q25b, cmps_merged$q30, use = "complete.obs")

# 2. Does controlling for political interest eliminate the civic density effect on economic optimism?
model_economic_controlled <- lm(q30_optim ~ opc + q25b + race_factor + gender_factor + 
                               income_factor + education_factor + region_factor + 
                               urban_factor + pid7, data = young_sample)

# 3. Does controlling for economic optimism eliminate the civic density effect on political interest?
model_political_controlled <- lm(q25b ~ opc + q30_optim + race_factor + gender_factor + 
                                income_factor + education_factor + region_factor + 
                                urban_factor + pid7, data = young_sample)

summary(model_economic_controlled)
summary(model_political_controlled)

#Minimal Model Check
# 2. Does controlling for political interest eliminate the civic density effect on economic pessimism?
minimal_economic_controlled <- lm(q30_optim ~ opc + q25b + race_factor + gender_factor + 
                               income_ordinal + pid7, data = young_sample)

# 3. Does controlling for economic pessimism eliminate the civic density effect on political interest?
minimal_political_controlled <- lm(q25b ~ opc + q30_optim + race_factor + gender_factor + 
                                income_ordinal + pid7, data = young_sample)

summary(minimal_economic_controlled)
summary(minimal_political_controlled)

# 1. Does the economic pessimism effect disappear across all ages when controlling for political interest?
minimal_economic_interaction_controlled <- lm(q30_optim ~ opc * age_c + q25b + race_factor + gender_factor + 
                                             income_ordinal + pid7, data = cmps_merged)

# 2. Does the political interest effect persist across all ages when controlling for economic pessimism?
minimal_political_interaction_controlled <- lm(q25b ~ opc * age_c + q30_optim + race_factor + gender_factor + 
                                              income_ordinal + pid7, data = cmps_merged)
summary(minimal_economic_interaction_controlled)
summary(minimal_political_interaction_controlled)
# We also examined whether the stronger relationship between civic opportunity structure and news-following among younger respondents might reflect heightened pessimism about household economic circumstances. Evidence for this interpretation is limited. In supplementary OLS models of the broader q30 response scale, opportunity structure is not significantly associated with pessimism in either the under-40 sample or the full sample with an age interaction. Although a binary logit predicting the pessimistic response category yields a positive association between opportunity structure and pessimism, that relationship is stronger among older respondents rather than younger ones. Taken together, these analyses provide little consistent support for pessimism as the mechanism underlying the age-conditional relationship between opportunity structure and political attentiveness

#Higher civic opportunity structure is associated with a lower likelihood of optimism, and that negative association becomes stronger as age increases. That is the mirror image of what you found for pessimism, which is what we would expect if the coding and modeling are behaving sensibly. Substantive interpretation. Because this is a logistic regression where 1 = optimistic: a negative coefficient on opc means higher opc is associated with lower odds of optimism; a negative interaction means this optimism-reducing association of opc is more negative for older respondents. So again, this does not support the idea that the youth effect in your news-following model is driven by younger people in high-opc places being uniquely less optimistic. Instead, the age pattern again points the other way: If higher-opc contexts are associated with lower optimism, that relationship is stronger among older respondents, not younger respondents.


#Although civic opportunity structure is associated with more negative economic outlooks in some specifications, these effects are stronger among older respondents. By contrast, the relationship between opportunity structure and more frequent news-following is strongest among younger respondents. This divergence suggests that the age-conditional attentiveness effect is unlikely to be driven primarily by pessimism or declining optimism among younger adults.

#Civic opportunity structure is associated not only with greater political attentiveness, but also with somewhat greater economic pessimism. However, the age pattern differs across the two outcomes. While opportunity structure is more strongly associated with news-following among younger respondents, it is more strongly associated with pessimism among older respondents. This suggests that increased pessimism is unlikely to be the primary reason why the attentiveness effect of opportunity structure is strongest among the young.
```

```{r Step 4: Create Plots and Tables with Various Model Specifications, include=TRUE}
model_comparison_turnout <- modelplot(
```

```{r Step 5: Turnout Visualizations, include=TRUE}
# Define model lists
turnout_models_ols <- list(
  "Bivariate OLS" = model_vote_2024,
  "OLS Regression w/Controls" = model_minimal
)

coef_ols <- imap_dfr(
  turnout_models_ols,
  ~ tidy(.x, conf.int = TRUE) |> mutate(model = .y)
) |>
  filter(term %in% c("opc", "opc:age_c")) |>
  mutate(
    term = recode(
      term,
      "opc" = "Civic Density"
    ),
    shape_group = case_when(
      grepl("Bivariate", model) ~ "Bivariate",
      grepl("Controls", model) ~ "Controlled"
    ),
    model = factor(
      model,
      levels = c(
        "Bivariate OLS",
        "OLS Regression w/Controls"
      )
    )
  )

p_coef_ols <- ggplot(
  coef_ols,
  aes(x = estimate, y = model, shape = shape_group)
) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "black") +
  geom_errorbarh(
    aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
    height = 0.2,
    color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, color = "gray50") +
  facet_wrap(~term, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c(
      "Bivariate" = 16,
      "Controlled" = 15,
      "Interaction" = 17
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Baseline turnout models (OLS)",
    x = "Coefficient estimate",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

p_coef_ols

model_agefactor_logit <- glm(
  voted_2024 ~ opc * age_factor + race_factor + gender_factor +
    income_ordinal + pid7,
  family = binomial,
  data = cmps_merged
)
model.frame(model_agefactor_logit)$age_factor |> levels()

age_levels_used <- levels(model.frame(model_agefactor_logit)$age_factor)

me_agefactor <- slopes(
  model_agefactor_logit,
  variables = "opc",
  newdata = datagrid(age_factor = age_levels_used),
  type = "response"
)

age_gradient_plot <- ggplot(me_agefactor, aes(x = age_factor, y = estimate)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "black") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = 0.15, color = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, color = "gray50") +
  labs(
    x = "Age group",
    y = "Marginal effect of opc on predicted turnout",
    title = "Effect of civic opportunity structure by age group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggsave(
  filename = "agegradientplot.png",
  plot = age_gradient_plot,
  width = 8,
  height = 6,
  dpi = 300
)

)

  ) +
  theme_minimal()


slopes_turnout <- slopes(
  turnout_logit_full,
  variables = "opc",

                                 max(cmps_merged$age_c, na.rm = TRUE),

  type = "response"
)

age_predictedpr_plot <- ggplot(slopes_turnout, aes(x = age_c, y = estimate)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +

  ) +

)
```
